description: The hand-verified expected result for the negative Gitleaks fixture that carries one record whose File names no location. Every value was derived by reading the fixture and the authored contracts in harness/lib/normalize/, never by running the adapter and recording what it printed. Where this file and harness/lib/normalize/adapters/gitleaks.py disagree, the disagreement is the finding: diagnose it rather than overwriting this file to match. The fixture's name states the class its element exercises -- absent_path -- and it did not always: it was called reject-gitleaks-unresolvable-path.json until the change that added a fixture genuinely asserting that other class. fixture_rename below records what was renamed and why, and keeps the derivation that established which of the two classes any record content can reach.
scanner_class_note: Fixed per tool by AAP 0.5.4's class table and authored as a constant in the adapter (SCANNER_CLASS). Trivy is the single tool whose class varies per record; this one never does, so no row below takes its class from record content, and the rejected record does not change the class of anything.
rules: No user-specified rule governs this file. review_rules returns exactly one line, 'No user rules provided.', which is the whole document; AAP 0.7 says the same. No rule is cited or invented here, and the absence is not licence to lower the bar -- the bar on this file is two things at once: a security property, stated under redaction_invariant and asserted against this file's own bytes, and a rejection class asserted against the module that defines it rather than against the fixture's file name.

fixture.derivation: A negative fixture is derived from the captured one rather than being an excerpt of it, so the provenance is stated as a derivation. Four of the five elements are byte-equal to elements of the positive fixture -- /0 to its element 1, /1 to its element 2, /3 to its element 3 and /4 to its element 5 -- established by comparing each element's serialization key by key and in key order, not by eye. The fifth, /2, is the defective record: it is the raw artifact's sole captured record with exactly two keys changed, its File emptied and the file component of its Fingerprint removed, so the only thing wrong with it is that it names no location.
fixture.defective_element_derivation_check: The other sixteen keys of /2 are byte-identical to the raw record's, and its key order is the raw record's key order, so a reviewer can re-derive the derivation by diffing /2 against harness/artifacts/raw/gitleaks.json's single element and finding exactly those two differences. The path that record carried before its File was emptied is deliberately not reproduced anywhere in this file; see rejections[0].no_guessed_path for why.
fixture.captured_provenance: No element is carried verbatim. /0, /1, /3 and /4 are the positive fixture's own derived elements, reused unchanged so that the surviving rows of this fixture are the same rows that file already fixes; /2 is this fixture's own derivation from the captured record. The recorded sha256 above is what makes a later edit to the fixture visible: these values are re-derived when the fixture changes, never adjusted to keep a test green.
fixture.not_records: There is nothing in this artifact that is not a record. The top level is an array of five objects and every one of them is a finding record; the count unit is the element, so no reading of this document can arrive at any number other than five.

routing.detected_by: normalize.shape.is_sarif returns false -- a SARIF artifact is a version of '2.1.0' together with a runs array, and those two together are the whole test. A bare array carries neither, and cannot: a JSON array has no string keys to look either of them up under.
routing.routing_decision: normalize.shape.route('gitleaks', doc) returns tool 'gitleaks', shape 'native', adapter 'gitleaks', scanner_class 'secret'
routing.not_a_shape_failure: No normalize.shape.UnknownArtifactShape is expected here, and a test asserting one against this fixture would be asserting the wrong thing. The enclosing document is a well-formed Gitleaks artifact and routes cleanly; exactly one record inside it is defective, and the adapter rejects that record while still emitting the other four. The fixtures that own shape-detection failure are near-sarif-version-only.json, near-sarif-runs-only.json and unknown-shape.json.
routing.the_document_level_fault_this_fixture_is: adapters/gitleaks.py raises GitleaksAdapterError rather than rejecting where the top level is not an array, because reconcile.count_records counts zero records in a non-array document and a rejection would then make rows plus rejections exceed the record count. That behaviour belongs to a call-level assertion, not to this fixture, whose top level is an array.
routing.negative_routing_test: The mandated negative routing assertion -- that a native artifact must not route to the SARIF adapter -- belongs to test_shape_routing_negative.py. This fixture is a legitimate subject for it in principle, since a bare array is the shape a permissive detector most obviously mis-reads, but the assertion is that test's to make and this file fixes only what the gitleaks adapter produces.

field_order_authority: harness/lib/normalize/emit.py, the FIELDS constant. Every row below carries all twelve keys in that order, present-with-null rather than omitted. adapters/gitleaks.py keeps an authored copy of the same tuple because it may not import emit; the two were compared and are identical.
absence_convention: Absence is JSON null here and in findings.json, and an empty field in findings.csv. tool, scanner_class, rule_id, message, severity_norm, path and in_scope are never absent -- emit.REQUIRED_FIELDS is exactly those seven -- which is why a record with no resolvable path has no valid row representation at all and is counted under a class instead.

allowlist.note: in_scope is decided by that file alone. The globs are not copied here: the allowlist is the single authority and stays byte-exact. The glob each row matched is recorded per row under row_derivations, and the one row matching none of them is named there too.

reference_behaviours.behaviour: a path rejection that is not the unresolvable_path class
reference_behaviours.what_this_file_fixes: One rejection under absent_path, with its sub-reason retained verbatim, alongside four rows the same artifact still produces.
reference_behaviours.why_it_belongs_here: The two path classes in paths.REJECT_CLASSES are easy to conflate, and a test that only counts rejections cannot tell them apart. This file fixes which one an empty File is, and fixture_rename fixes why the other one cannot be reached from record content at all.

reference_behaviours.behaviour: partial parse as a first-class outcome
reference_behaviours.what_this_file_fixes: rows 4, rejections 1, parse_status partial -- every parsable record emitted and the one defective record counted, rather than the artifact abandoned.
reference_behaviours.why_it_belongs_here: AAP 0.5.4 makes partial parse a first-class outcome. An adapter that stopped at the defective element would produce two rows and look plausible; the fixture puts the defect in the middle of the array precisely so that stopping early is visible in the row count.

reference_behaviours.behaviour: the invocation-dependent path base, on the rejection path as well as the row path
reference_behaviours.what_this_file_fixes: Every surviving path is the record's File taken against the base recorded for this runner, whose kind is scan_root, so the value is root-relative and unchanged; and the rejected record is rejected for having no File at all rather than for anything about the base.
reference_behaviours.why_it_belongs_here: A wrong base mis-resolves every Gitleaks row while every value still looks plausible, and it would also change which rejection class a defective record lands under. The base is therefore read from runner-metadata.json rather than inferred from the paths themselves, and resolution_context records what was read.

resolution_context.path_base_source: harness/artifacts/logs/runner-metadata.json, tools.gitleaks.path_base -- read as input, never assumed. Its record_path_field is 'File', which is the field resolve_gitleaks_path reads; the adapter's own _FILE_KEY is only the default that function falls back to.
resolution_context.path_base_value_note: The recorded base is the pinned scan root. Its absolute form is deliberately not reproduced here: no absolute path appears anywhere in this file, and these rows hold for whatever absolute root the adapter is given.
resolution_context.recorded_invocation_shape: Eighteen invocations, each handed exactly one root-relative directory, with the runner's working directory set to the scan root.
resolution_context.invocation_source: runner-metadata.json tools.gitleaks.invocation_form and working_directory -- invocations_per_run 18, target_passing_style 'exactly one root-relative path per invocation, one invocation per scope directory', working directory equal to the scan root -- corroborated independently by harness/bin/run-gitleaks.sh, which cds to the scan root and then loops one directory per invocation, and by harness/ENVIRONMENT.md's path-base table.
resolution_context.why_the_base_is_invocation_dependent: gitleaks dir takes exactly one path and reports relative to the process working directory when handed more, so the base is a property of the invocation rather than of the tool (AAP 0.5.4). Both shapes are real: the historical harness AAP 0.2.3 describes passed all eighteen scope directories to a single invocation, and this provisioning passes one per invocation. This is the one adapter where a fixture can be wrong about a path without looking wrong, which is why the base was read rather than assumed.
resolution_context.invariance_across_the_two_shapes: Here the two shapes give the same base, because the runner's working directory is the scan root: one root-relative directory per invocation reports File relative to that root, and eighteen paths in one invocation would report relative to the working directory, which is that same root. Every path below therefore holds under either reading. That is a fact about this provisioning, not a licence to skip reading the metadata -- a runner that cds elsewhere would need these paths re-derived, and no runner may be edited to make one shape true (AAP 0.3.2).
resolution_context.path_basis_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, BASIS_ALREADY_ROOT_RELATIVE -- the basis resolve_recorded_path records where the recorded base and the scan root are the same location, so the reported File was already root-relative and the join changed nothing. The basis says so rather than implying a resolution that did no work.
resolution_context.path_kind_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, path_kind_for: no '!' separator and no leading '..' segment, so every emitted path names a location inside the scanned tree. Whether the file exists on disk is a separate question paths.py never asks -- nothing in it stats the filesystem -- and each of the four surviving paths was checked against the pinned tree separately, per row.
resolution_context.severity_source: None. The eighteen keys a pinned-Gitleaks record carries include no severity-like field, and the fixture carries no Severity key anywhere, so every emitted row goes through severity.SeverityResult.absent().
resolution_context.severity_basis_authority: harness/lib/normalize/severity.py, BASIS_NO_VOCABULARY. absent() carries severity_native null, severity_norm Info and that basis, and its __post_init__ refuses a severity_native on it -- so the absence is structural rather than a convention a caller has to remember. Info is not hard-coded in the adapter.
resolution_context.severity_selected_entry_note: null on this path: nothing was used to derive the band, so there is neither a label nor a score entry to record. The band comes from a policy fixed before any output was observed, and no native literal is synthesised -- inventing one would put a literal into oss-scan-results/severity-map.md that the tool never emitted.
resolution_context.severity_map_consequence: The tally is fed once per emitted row and never for a rejected record, so severity-map.md can name gitleaks as a tool that defines no severity vocabulary with a row count behind the statement, and that count is four here rather than five. A rejected record contributing a tally entry would report an entry against a row the dataset does not contain.
resolution_context.package_coordinate: null on every row. A secret finding names a code location rather than a package, and this shape supplies no coordinate to carry. AAP 0.5.4's unformable-coordinate rejection reaches dependency-oriented records only, so the absence here is not a rejection condition -- not even on the row whose path is a lockfile.
resolution_context.cwe_and_cve: null on every row. The shape carries no weakness or advisory identifier; deriving a CWE from a rule id would be inference of exactly the kind AAP 0.5.4 forbids.

rejection_boundary.statement: A path that cannot be resolved at all is a rejection. A path that merely resolves somewhere unwanted is a kept row with in_scope false. This fixture carries one of each, deliberately: /2 names no location and is counted, and /4 names a real file outside the twelve globs and is kept.
rejection_boundary.why_it_can_only_be_a_rejection: path is one of only two never-absent fields in the twelve-field schema, the other being severity_norm: emit.REQUIRED_FIELDS carries path, and emit.OPTIONAL_FIELDS is exactly severity_native, start_line, cwe, cve and package_coordinate. A record with no path therefore has no valid row representation at all -- emit.py raises on a null path rather than writing one -- so counting it under a named class is the only outcome that neither drops the record nor invents a coordinate for it.

not_a_rejection.case: a path resolving outside the twelve authoritative globs
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with in_scope false, counted under rows_out_of_scope
not_a_rejection.evidence: The real out-of-glob files in the pinned tree include dev/package-lock.json, ui-test/package-lock.json and docs/Gemfile.lock. Each resolves to a tree_file path and is kept; out of scope means kept and marked, never rejected.
not_a_rejection.where: /4, which becomes rows[3] with in_scope false. Using an out-of-glob-but-real path as this fixture's defect would have asserted the opposite of what AAP 0.8.3 requires, so the fixture carries one as a kept row instead -- the distinction made visible in the same document rather than argued about.

not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with in_scope false, counted in non_filesystem_paths
not_a_rejection.evidence: Serialized as <container-relative-to-root>!<member> with '!' the single separator, and with ../ segments preserved rather than normalized where the container lies outside the root. A well-formed Gitleaks File value carrying '!' takes exactly that route through resolve_recorded_path and becomes a row; one whose container cannot be serialized -- a URI-scheme container, say -- is a malformed_record, which is a third outcome again and not this class.

not_a_rejection.case: a path in a src/test tree
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with in_scope false
not_a_rejection.evidence: The exclusion is literal -- a path containing src/test is out of scope -- and it removes the path from scope rather than from the dataset. No path in this fixture contains it, including the Python test module, whose test-ness is a tests/ directory and a test_ filename rather than a Maven src/test tree.

not_a_rejection.case: a path naming a file that does not exist on disk
not_a_rejection.expected: a kept row with in_scope decided by the globs alone
not_a_rejection.evidence: Nothing in paths.py stats the filesystem, so resolution is textual: a syntactically ordinary relative File resolves to a tree_file path whether or not a file is there. Existence is a question run-record.md answers separately, by counting such rows against the same root. All four surviving paths here do exist at the pin, recorded per row.

rejection_boundary.defective_record_resolves_to_nothing: Verified from the fixture rather than assumed. /2's File is the empty string: it is not a relative reference, not an absolute path, carries no '!' separator and names no archive container, so there is no reading of it that yields a location. resolve_recorded_path's first test is exactly this -- a null or blank value -- and it precedes every base-kind branch, so the outcome does not depend on the recorded base and could not be changed by any base. No external-but-resolvable coordinate is recorded as the rejected record here, because recording one would assert the opposite of what this fixture exists to assert.
rejection_boundary.no_guessed_path: The rejected record is rejected and counted, never given a path. Nothing in this file supplies a coordinate for it, not even a plausible one, and not even the one its captured ancestor carried.

fixture_rename.summary: This fixture and this expected file were renamed. The fixture asserts absent_path and was called reject-gitleaks-unresolvable-path.json, so its name stated a class it does not produce -- and the class it named was, at that time, exercised by no committed fixture at all. Both halves are now fixed: this pair carries the class it asserts in its name, and a new fixture carries the other one.
fixture_rename.the_bytes_did_not_change: Only the names. The fixture's sha256 and byte count recorded above are the same values the previous expected file recorded, which is checkable: the rename was performed with mv and no field of any record was touched. Renaming the file was the correct repair precisely because the fixture was never wrong -- its name was.
fixture_rename.why_the_old_name_was_wrong: AAP 0.5.4 enumerates the rejection conditions in a list whose first entry is 'an unresolvable or absent path' -- one condition covering both -- and the old name named that condition. paths.py implements it as two members of its closed ten-name vocabulary, REJECT_ABSENT_PATH and REJECT_UNRESOLVABLE_PATH, reached by two different branches and carrying two different details. A fixture for the condition therefore exercises one of the two halves, and a name that does not say which leaves a reader to infer the wrong one -- which is what a reviewer did.

what_now_owns_the_other_class.how_it_reaches_the_class: One sound captured record read under a runner-metadata document recording path_base.kind 'none'. That is the only route to the class for this adapter, as the branch-space derivation below establishes, so the fixture's definition includes the metadata it is read under.
what_now_owns_the_other_class.why_it_had_to_be_added: AAP 0.9.4 requires a negative fixture and an assertion for every rejection condition each exercised adapter can produce, whether or not this run's artifacts contained the case. Before it, unresolvable_path was reached in this module only by a test that built its own record in memory -- a committed assertion with no committed input.

fixture_rename.expected_class_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, the REJECT_ABSENT_PATH constant, whose own comment reads 'An absent path: the record carries no path field, or carries an empty one.' Written verbatim as spelled there, and to be asserted against the module rather than against this string by eye.
fixture_rename.corroborating_sibling: oss-scan-results/adapter-tests/expected/reject-gitleaks-malformed-record.rows.json reaches the same reading independently, in its behaviours_not_exercised_by_this_fixture list: 'A record with an absent or empty File. That is the absent_path class, and reject-gitleaks-absent-path.json owns it.' And expected/reject-gitleaks-unresolvable-path.rows.json states the other half from its own side, under path_policy.the_fixture_names_the_class_it_asserts. Three documents derived separately from the same fixtures and the same contracts agree, which is worth more than any one of them asserting it alone.
fixture_rename.absent_check_precedence_consequence: In resolve_recorded_path the blank-value test is the first statement, before the bytecode-class guard, before the 'none' base branch, before archive handling and before any join. So /2 is absent_path under every one of the eight path_base kinds the metadata vocabulary declares. There is no configuration of this pipeline in which that element is unresolvable_path.

unresolvable_path_is_unreachable_from_re.claim: Under the recorded base -- kind scan_root, with a base value present -- no File value of any shape produces unresolvable_path. The class is reachable only from the metadata, never from a record.
unresolvable_path_is_unreachable_from_re.method: Every branch of resolve_recorded_path was enumerated from the source and each was exercised with a representative File value against the real ToolPathBase built from runner-metadata.json. The outcomes below are the complete branch space for this tool; a reader can re-derive each from the function's body.

branch_space.file_value_shape: absent, null, empty or all whitespace
present but not a string -- a number, a list, an object

branch_space.outcome: a row, kind tree_file, basis already-root-relative

branch_space.file_value_shape: an absolute path inside the root
branch_space.outcome: a row, kind tree_file, basis absolute-relativized-to-root

branch_space.file_value_shape: an absolute path outside the root, or a relative one beginning with ..
branch_space.outcome: a row, kind outside_root, with its ../ segments preserved

branch_space.file_value_shape: an archive reference carrying one '!', with either a relative or an absolute container
branch_space.outcome: a row, kind archive_member, serialized against the root

branch_space.file_value_shape: an archive-like reference whose container cannot be serialized -- a URI-scheme container, say
a URI-form string with no '!' at all, such as a urn reference
branch_space.outcome: paths.PathPolicyError is raised by the emitted-path invariant rather than returned as a rejection. A caller fault surfaces loudly; it is not this class either.

branch_space.file_value_shape: a syntactically ordinary path naming a file that is not on disk
branch_space.outcome: a row, kind tree_file -- nothing in paths.py stats the filesystem

unresolvable_path_is_unreachable_from_re.conclusion: absent_path, malformed_record, a row, or a raised error. unresolvable_path appears nowhere in the branch space, so no edit to this fixture could have produced it and none was attempted.
unresolvable_path_is_unreachable_from_re.why_this_derivation_is_kept: It is what establishes that the other class needed a metadata-level fixture rather than a defective record, and therefore why the new fixture is shaped the way it is. Removing it with the rename would discard the reasoning and leave the new fixture's shape looking arbitrary.

fixture_rename.where_unresolvable_path_is_reachable: From a ToolPathBase whose kind is 'none', which runner-metadata.json's own path_base_kind_vocabulary annotates: 'No explicit base could be established from the runner. paths.py must reject such a record under unresolvable_path rather than fall back.' That is a property of the recorded metadata, not of any record, and this provisioning's gitleaks entry records scan_root with a base value. The other routes to the class -- a per_section_target base with no section base supplied, and a degenerate SARIF uriBaseId chain -- belong to trivy and to the SARIF producers, whose own fixtures cover them.

metadata_variant_expectation.scenario: This same five-element fixture adapted with a ToolPathBase for gitleaks whose kind is 'none' and whose base_value is null, everything else unchanged. It is recorded because it is the tally a reader would predict and get wrong, and because it shows why the new unresolvable_path fixture holds one element rather than five.
metadata_variant_expectation.expected_unresolvable_detail: the runner metadata records path_base.kind 'none' for 'gitleaks': no explicit base could be established from the runner, and the document's own instruction is to reject such a record rather than fall back
metadata_variant_expectation.counters: every key of adapters.gitleaks.COUNTER_KEYS is 0, since no record reaches severity, in_scope or a path kind, and no element names a second location
metadata_variant_expectation.note: The absent_path rejection in that tally is /2 again, unchanged -- which is the precedence point above made concrete: even where the base itself is unresolvable, the element with no File is still counted for having no File. A test asserting five unresolvable_path rejections in this scenario would be asserting something the module does not do.
metadata_variant_expectation.not_a_substitute_for_this_file: This block fixes a scenario, not this fixture's expected result. rows, rejections, counts and counters below are the expected result, and they are the ones a loader reading these files generically consumes.
metadata_variant_expectation.superseded_as_the_way_to_assert_the_clas: It is no longer the scenario a test asserting unresolvable_path for this adapter should use. fixtures/reject-gitleaks-unresolvable-path.json is, because a committed fixture is inspectable and a scenario is not. This block remains as the derivation of the mixed tally -- four unresolvable_path and one absent_path from the same document -- which the new single-element fixture deliberately avoids: a mixed tally makes neither class attributable to a single record.

fixture_rename.nothing_was_edited_to_reconcile_the_two: No file was edited to make the names agree with the classes: the fixture was renamed and a second fixture was added. The adapter and paths.py are unchanged -- they implement the AAP's condition as two classes, which is a finer distinction than the AAP's own wording and therefore no contradiction of it. runner-metadata.json is unchanged and must stay so: it is the gate's record of the provisioning as it was found, so editing its path_base to make a class reachable would falsify a record this run is required to preserve, which is why the new fixture supplies its own metadata document instead.
fixture_rename.how_a_test_should_assert_this: Assert the class against the module -- that the single rejection's reject_class is paths.REJECT_ABSENT_PATH and is a member of paths.REJECT_CLASSES -- rather than against a name parsed out of the fixture's filename. A test that derived its expectation from the filename would fail for the right value and pass only once someone had made the module wrong.

counts.raw_count_unit: one element of the top-level array -- the unit normalize.reconcile.count_records walks independently of row construction; its _count_gitleaks is the array's length and nothing else
counts.raw_count_authority: normalize.reconcile.count_records('gitleaks', doc), which builds no row, resolves no path and maps no severity. It is the independent half of the identity: a count taken from the traversal that builds the rows would satisfy the assertion while testing nothing. For this shape it also means the count is unaffected by any record's content -- a defective element counts exactly like a sound one, which is what makes the arithmetic below a real check.
counts.rejections_by_class_note: One class, one record, and the class is the one the fixture's name states -- which it did not always: the fixture was renamed from reject-gitleaks-unresolvable-path.json precisely so that this block and the filename agree without a reader having to read a reconciliation first. fixture_rename records the rename and keeps the derivation that established which of the two path classes any record content can reach.
counts.every_element_yields_exactly_one_outcome: One row or one rejection per element, never both and never neither -- _adapt_record returns a single value of one of the two types, so the property is structural rather than asserted. Four elements carry a non-empty RuleID and Description, a non-empty File and a StartLine that is an integer of at least 1, and become rows; the fifth carries no File and is counted.
counts.parse_status_authority: harness/lib/normalize/cli.py, PARSE_STATUS_PARTIAL = 'partial', assigned as partial where there are rejections and clean where there are none. Partial is right precisely because the adapter did not abandon the artifact: every parsable record was emitted and the one rejected record is counted under its class, with its parser reason retained. This is deliberately not normalize.reconcile's STATUS_PASS / STATUS_FAIL / STATUS_NOT_APPLICABLE vocabulary, which describes an assertion's outcome rather than an artifact's parse.
counts.row_order: fixture order, preserved, with the rejected element contributing nothing to it -- so rows[2] comes from element /3 and rows[3] from /4. Both output files use this order and emit.py compares them ordered row by row, so an expected file in any other order would assert something the pipeline does not promise.
counts.defect_position_is_deliberate: The defective element sits at /2, in the middle of the array rather than at either end, so an adapter that stopped on the first defect would emit two rows and an adapter that skipped the tail would emit three. Both would be visible in the row count above.

counters_authority: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/gitleaks.py, COUNTER_KEYS as returned by new_counters(): six authored keys, then one path_kind_* per normalize.paths.PATH_KINDS member and one severity_basis_* per normalize.severity.BASIS_VALUES member -- fifteen keys in that order, which is the key set and the order above. Deliberately absent from it, and so from here: any adapter-side count of records walked, rows or rejections. Those are len(rows), len(rejections) and reconcile.count_records, and a plausible substitute published here is how the independent-traversal requirement would quietly be lost.
counters_note: Four numbers here are 4 and not 5, and that is the classification order made visible rather than a miscount: the rejected element never reaches severity, never reaches the in_scope decision and never contributes a path kind, because the path step precedes all three and it does not get past it. So severity_absent, severity_basis_no_vocabulary and path_kind_tree_file are 4, and rows_in_scope plus rows_out_of_scope is 3 + 1 = 4 -- one measurement split, not a second count of the same thing. multi_location_records is the one counter a rejected record could still have incremented, since the adapter takes it before the path step; it is 0 here because SymlinkFile is the empty string on all five elements, including /2.

counters_aap_0_5_4_reported.note: The four counters AAP 0.5.4 has reported per tool. Two of them -- multi_location_records and non_filesystem_paths -- are keys of this adapter's own counter set and appear above with the same values. The other two are not: a Gitleaks record carries no CWE or CVE field at all, so no record can be multi-valued in either, and the adapter keys no counter it could never increment. They are stated here as 0 by construction so the four required numbers are all present in one place, and so that the difference between 'measured 0' and '0 because the field does not exist in this shape' is legible rather than inferred from a missing key.

redaction_invariant.requirement: AAP 0.5.4: Gitleaks runs with redaction so a matched secret's value never enters an artifact, and no adapter carries a secret value into any field. This file is committed to git -- .gitignore line 31 matches artifacts/ and nothing under oss-scan-results/ -- so the invariant has to hold of this file as written, not only of the dataset the adapter produces. A negative expected file carries one exposure a positive one does not: a rejection detail, which AAP 0.5.4 requires retained verbatim and which is therefore quoted here in full.
redaction_invariant.message_source_on_every_row: Description, the rule's own description. Never Secret, never Match, and never Message, which is a git commit message rather than a description. There is deliberately no fallback: every candidate would either infer content the tool did not state or carry a captured value into the field.
redaction_invariant.keys_never_read_authority: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/gitleaks.py, NEVER_READ_FIELDS. Fingerprint is excluded even though this artifact's values are file-rule-line composites: in commit mode it also carries a commit identity, and a field whose safety depends on which mode ran is not a field to read.
redaction_invariant.keys_read_authority: harness/lib/normalize/adapters/gitleaks.py, SOURCE_FIELDS -- the four keys a row is built from, named one at a time. The record is never copied, spread or iterated into a row, which is what makes the invariant structural there; here it is upheld by deriving each of the twelve values from those four keys and fixed constants alone.
redaction_invariant.rejection_detail_safety: The rejected record's detail is quoted verbatim below and names no value from the record: paths.py composes it from the metadata's record_path_field name and fixed prose. The adapter's own rejection paths go further -- _safe_value_repr renders only None, a bool, an int and a float and otherwise names a value's type -- so no string from any key, expected or not, can reach a detail. That is why the quoted detail is safe to commit.
redaction_invariant.record_identity_safety: The rejection's record_identity carries RuleID, StartLine and the File field twice, once under its own name and once as reported_path. All three are identifying fields rather than captured values, and the File value in this record is the empty string, so the identity below discloses nothing at all about a secret.
redaction_invariant.symlink_file_is_the_one_exception: SymlinkFile is the single key outside SOURCE_FIELDS the adapter looks at, and only through a predicate returning a bool. It is a filesystem path rather than a captured value, it is never emitted, and it is never substituted for an absent File -- which matters more in this fixture than in any other, since /2 is exactly the record a substitution would have rescued into a wrongly-pathed row. It is empty on all five elements here, so it decides nothing beyond leaving multi_location_records at 0.
redaction_invariant.check_performed: Every distinct Match, Secret and Fingerprint value in the fixture -- seven values across the five elements -- was tested as a substring against the whole of this file. Zero hits, which is the required result. The check covers prose as well as row fields, and three drafting consequences follow from it: no sentence here quotes the placeholder string the runner's redaction flag substitutes for a captured value, nowhere is a path, a rule id and a line number joined into one colon-separated string, since that is the shape of this artifact's fingerprint values, and the defective element's fingerprint remnant is likewise never reproduced -- which is a second, independent reason not to write its rule id and line adjacent to one another.
redaction_invariant.upstream_protection_is_not_the_check: The runner passes a redaction flag, so a captured value never reached the artifact in the first place. That is upstream protection in a runner this run may not edit, and it is not a substitute for the assertion above, which is made against this file's own bytes.

prohibitions_observed.no_cross_tool_interpretation: Trivy's adapter also reports secrets. A location both tools report is two rows in two expected files with no comment: nothing here compares tools, ranks them, explains why one found something another did not, or folds one into the other (AAP 0.3.2). The rejected record is likewise not compared with anything any other tool did or did not report about the same code.
prohibitions_observed.no_judging: No row is characterised as real, important, a false positive or a duplicate, and no row's rule or location is glossed as the sort of thing that tends to be one. The rejected record is not judged either: it is counted for a structural reason -- it names no location -- and nothing here says whether what it reported was worth reporting.
prohibitions_observed.no_dedup: Two elements share a RuleID and a Description and both become rows; a third shares them and is rejected for its path alone. Three records, and no collapsing of any of them into the others.
prohibitions_observed.no_invented_severity: The tool defines no severity vocabulary, so none is invented: severity_native stays null and severity_norm comes from the fixed no-vocabulary policy rather than from a guess at what a finding deserves. The rejected record gets no severity at all, not even a default.
prohibitions_observed.kept_not_filtered: The out-of-glob lockfile row is kept with in_scope false and counted, never dropped (AAP 0.9.3). Only evidence about the runner establishes a wrong scan root (AAP 0.8.3), and the recorded metadata shows this runner resolved the pinned root.
prohibitions_observed.rejected_not_dropped: The defective record is counted under a named class with its sub-reason retained, not silently discarded. A dropped record would leave rows plus rejections short of the independent record count, which is the arithmetic that makes silent dropping detectable.
prohibitions_observed.never_derived_by_running_the_adapter: Every value in this file was read out of the fixture and the authored contracts -- the fixture's five elements, adapters/gitleaks.py's five-step classification order and counter set, paths.py's rejection vocabulary and resolver branches, emit.py's field order and absence convention, severity.py's no-vocabulary result, reconcile.py's count unit and cli.py's parse-status vocabulary. Nothing here was produced by invoking the adapter and recording its output, which would make the test a tautology: the adapter would be asserted to agree with itself. The class divergence above is the clearest evidence of the difference -- it was found by reading resolve_recorded_path, and a file written from a run would have recorded the same class with no explanation of why the filename disagrees.
prohibitions_observed.agreement_check_disclosed: After these values were derived and written, the adapter was invoked over this fixture once with the real metadata, root and allowlist, and its rows, rejections, detail, record identity and counters compared to what is recorded here; agreement was complete. The metadata-variant scenario under fixture_rename was checked the same way, once. Both checks followed derivation, could only ever have surfaced a disagreement to diagnose, and contributed no value to this file. A reader who wants the derivation checked should check it against the fixture and the contracts, which is what every row_derivations entry below is for.

corroboration.defective_element_has_no_counterpart: The rejected record has nothing to corroborate against and needs nothing: it appears in no other fixture, contributes no dataset row, and its expected outcome is checkable by reading the fixture and resolve_recorded_path. rejections.locator_note: The pointer and the array index name the same element. Both are this document's coordinates: paths.py builds this rejection directly rather than through make_rejection, so the produced Rejection carries no record_index and its record_identity is what a test must locate the record by. A test comparing identities should therefore compare the four keys below, and find the element by its index itself.
rejections.reject_class_authority: harness/lib/normalize/paths.py, the REJECT_ABSENT_PATH constant -- a literal member of paths.REJECT_CLASSES, the closed set of ten. Written verbatim rather than paraphrased, and to be asserted against the module rather than by eye: a test that only counts rejections cannot tell one condition from another, so the class name is what carries the assertion. The sibling class unresolvable_path is owned by fixtures/reject-gitleaks-unresolvable-path.json, which reaches it from the recorded metadata rather than from record content; fixture_rename states why no record content here could have reached it.
rejections.classification_step: step 4 of the adapter's fixed classification order -- shape, rule identifier, message, path, start_line. Steps 1 to 3 all pass on this record: it is a JSON object, it carries a non-empty string RuleID, and it carries a non-empty string Description. That is deliberate, so the only thing left to reject it for is its path.
rejections.multi_location_check_ran: The adapter takes the multi-location count before the path step, so this record was inspected for a second location and found to name none -- SymlinkFile is the empty string. Worth stating because it is the one counter a rejected record can still move.
rejections.start_line_never_examined: Step 5 is never reached, so this record's StartLine is never examined and non_integer_start_line is not in play. Worth stating because the fixture does give the defective record a StartLine, and a reader could otherwise expect an interaction between the two conditions.
rejections.file_value_note: The empty string, not a missing key. Both are the same class: paths.py's first test treats an absent key, a null, an empty string and an all-whitespace string alike, on the ground that none of them names a location. The fixture uses the empty string because that is what removing a value from this shape leaves behind -- the key is one of the tool's eighteen and a real record always carries it.
rejections.expected_detail: the record carries no File value, so it names no location; path is not an optional field
rejections.expected_detail_note: The detail is the sub-reason AAP 0.5.4 requires a rejection to carry, and it is quoted in full because every rejection class in this pipeline covers several routes: naming the class alone would not distinguish this record from one whose File was a number. The field name in it is not a constant -- paths.py composes it from the metadata's record_path_field -- so a test may assert the detail by its distinguishing substrings rather than by full-string equality. It contains no value from the record; see redaction_invariant.rejection_detail_safety.
rejections.record_identity_note: resolve_gitleaks_path supplies RuleID, StartLine and the metadata-named path field; resolve_recorded_path then adds reported_path as the raw value it was handed, which for this record is the same empty string. Enough to find the record in the artifact again, and never the record itself and never a secret value. Note that the identity carries the record's StartLine even though the classification never examined it -- an identifying field is not an examined one.
rejections.why_not_a_row: There is no path to put in the row. path is never absent from a row, so a record whose File names nothing has no valid row representation, and the alternatives -- dropping it, or substituting its SymlinkFile, or giving it the path its captured ancestor carried -- would each either hide it or assert a location the record does not state. Counting it under a named class keeps it visible and keeps the arithmetic honest.
rejections.contributes_no_severity_literal: The rejected record is never fed to the severity tally, so no entry from it reaches severity-map.md. That document reports against the rows the dataset contains, and this record contributes none -- which is why severity_absent is 4 rather than 5.
rejections.contributes_to_no_path_or_scope_counter: It reaches neither a path kind nor the in_scope decision, so every path_kind_* counter and both rows_in_scope and rows_out_of_scope exclude it.
rejections.no_guessed_path: No coordinate is supplied for this record anywhere in this file, not even a plausible one, and not the one its captured ancestor carried before its File was emptied. A reviewer wanting that value has harness/artifacts/raw/gitleaks.json; an expected file that reproduced it would be asserting a path for a record the adapter must refuse to path.
rejections.not_produced_by_any_other_condition: The eleven sibling reject-gitleaks-* fixtures own the other five conditions this adapter can produce -- malformed_record, missing_rule_id, missing_message over four documents, non_integer_start_line over four, and unresolvable_path -- and this record meets none of them: it is an object, its RuleID and Description are non-empty strings, and its StartLine is never read. Its File is the empty string, which is this fixture's own class rather than unresolvable_path, whose single document reaches that class through a recorded base and not through record content. So this fixture re-covers nothing they cover, and each of them still has its own work to do.

in_scope_verification.method: Each of the four surviving paths was matched against the twelve globs by hand and then checked twice more, with two implementations that are not the one under test: a glob-to-regex translation written for this check, and CPython 3.13's PurePosixPath.full_match, whose ** spans zero or more directories. All three agree on all four paths, and on which glob each matched.
in_scope_verification.why_not_fnmatch: Three of the twelve globs depend on ** matching zero or more directories, and neither fnmatch nor PurePath.match provides those semantics. A matcher built on either silently drops whole modules, and a silently dropped module looks exactly like a module with nothing to report (AAP 0.5.4).
in_scope_verification.src_test_rule: The exclusion is the literal substring src/test. No path here contains it, including the Python test module, whose test-ness is expressed as a tests/ directory and a test_ filename rather than a Maven src/test tree.
in_scope_verification.the_rejected_record_is_not_in_this_check: in_scope is a property of a resolved path, and the rejected record has none, so it is neither in scope nor out of scope -- it is counted. A file that recorded in_scope false for it would be asserting that the allowlist had been consulted about a path that was never produced.
